newsitem.title: UK: Europe's freeze kills scores, ice blocks waterways.
newsitem.headline: Europe's freeze kills scores, ice blocks waterways.

text.p: Europe's big freeze was blamed for scores of deaths, ice blocked waterways across the continent and forecasters warned on Thursday of more severe weather to come.

Among the few to celebrate the freak low temperatures were Dutch fans of a rarely-staged ice skating marathon, and traders holding oil futures, whose prices rose on expectations of increased European demand for energy.
The February contract for Brent crude oil on London's International Petroleum Exchange was up 56 cents a barrel at $24.37 on Thursday morning from its 1996 closing price.
In France, where at least 15 people have died from the cold in the last few days, some 30 homeless people burst into an exclusive hotel to protest at their plight.
They glued a wooden plaque to the marble floor of the Grand Hotel in Paris inscribed: "To those who died of cold".
Among the casualties of the weather were a woman killed and 16 people injured in a huge traffic pileup caused by ice on Italy's main north-south motorway near the town of Modena.

In Germany and Britain, New Year revellers died of cold outdoors after drinking. The weather was also blamed for some deaths among people in their own unheated homes, like that of a 53-year-old man in Antwerp, Belgium.
Eastern Germany experienced overnight temperatures of as low as minus 26 degrees Celsius (minus 15 Fahrenheit) and Belgium a record low of minus 21 Celsius (minus eight Fahrenheit).
One man was killed and another was seriously injured in an avalanche in northeastern Italy and meteorologists warned more were likely.
In Courmayeur, northwest Italy, officials were monitoring conditions closely amid fears that more snow or temperature changes could unleash a 25,000 cubic metre mass of snow and ice.

"The situation is under control, there should be no panic. In any case, any cautionary measures can be set in motion swiftly," the mayor of Courmayeur, Ferdinando Derriard, told Italian radio. "If there's a lot of snow, we will close the valley."
Rivers and canals across Europe were hit by the extreme cold.
Austrian shipping authorities said much of the Danube, Europe's busiest east-west waterway, remained closed.

"Everything is shut, from Germany right through to the Slovak Republic," said a spokesman for Vienna's river police. "If the weather stays like this, it will take at least another week until the river reopens."
The Danube was covered by a sheet of ice up to 25 cm (10 in) thick in Vienna. Temperatures in Austria have plunged to their lowest levels in 30 years, claiming at least four lives.

Hungarian river authorites said the section of the Danube along the Slovak border was full of drift-ice, prompting ice breakers to be put on alert. Hungary's other main river, the Tisza, had a solid ice covering of between 10 cm (four in) and 30 cm (12 in).
Barge traffic on the Rhine was unaffected, but ice caused problems on some of its tributaries and canals.

Belgium's Meuse river was reported to be completely frozen over, stopping all movement of barges. An attempt to break the ice on Wednesday was abandoned because it was too cold to start the engines of specially adapted ice-breaking tugs.
Temperatures in Britain were less severe than on continental Europe but were still among the lowest for years. Meteorologists expected little respite across much of Europe before next week.

Britons rushed to bet on the weather, among them one woman who will collect 1,000 pounds ($1,700) in winnings if the River Thames freezes over in central London for the first time since 1814. A bookmaker offered her odds of 200-1.

The freezing weather brought jubilation for Dutch skaters as the organisers of the Elfstedentocht (Eleven Cities Tour) marathon said the event could be held on Saturday, for only the 15th time this century.
The 200-km (125 mile) race over a maze of canals and inland waterways, in which up to 16,000 skaters will take part, attracted over a million spectators in 1986.
Despite temperatures well below zero, snow flurries and icy winds, a group of hardy British swimmers took their annual New Year's day plunge off the coast of northeast England.
"It was bitterly cold in there, but nothing a good brandy couldn't put right," 27-year-old Katrina Gray told the Daily Mail.
